Key Concepts
Overview of functions used in class:

dim(): dimensions (i.e. rows x columns)
glimpse(): preview of dataset
head(): first few rows of dataset
filter(): selects rows of data based on given threshold
select(): selects specified columns
mutate(): add/create a new column
arrange(): rearrange rows in a new order (descending, ascending) based on a category
group_by(): changes the unit of analysis; sorts the data into specified categorization
case_when(): allows you sort data into multiple categories

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
In this analysis, I look at women whose income was below the poverty level in the past 12 months across counties in New York, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably. Data collected on vulnerable populations can be used both to understand and provide necessary resources to those populations, so the reliability of the data is important for ensuring that those populations are accurately represented.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Choosing what to measure

my_state <- "NY"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B17001_017"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Pulling the data

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

Let’s look at what came back.

dim(county_data)

[1] 62  5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID NAME                         variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                        <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York      B17001_017    20723  1434
2 36003 Allegany County, New York    B17001_017     3616   350
3 36005 Bronx County, New York       B17001_017   211879  5751
4 36007 Broome County, New York      B17001_017    19066  1290
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York B17001_017     6786   535
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York      B17001_017     5499   528


The data includes 62 rows. This matches the total number of counties in the state of New York.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe/estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                        estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                          <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Hamilton County, New York        250    85    34  
 2 Wyoming County, New York        2364   439    18.6
 3 Yates County, New York          1780   300    16.9
 4 Washington County, New York     3436   566    16.5
 5 Greene County, New York         2803   461    16.4
 6 Orleans County, New York        2736   446    16.3
 7 Schuyler County, New York       1371   219    16.0
 8 Delaware County, New York       3123   467    15.0
 9 Fulton County, New York         3764   555    14.7
10 Cortland County, New York       3074   435    14.2


Hamilton County has the largest relative margin of error, at 34%.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence     8
2 Low confidence     35
3 Moderate           19


Eight counties out of the total 62 fall into the category of “High Confidence” when it is defined at a threshold margin of error of 5%. Nineteen counties fall into the category of “Moderate Confidence” when it is defined at a threshold of 10%. Thirty-five counties were classified as “Low Confidence.”

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York       20723   1434  315374    NA
2 36003 Allegany County, New York      3616    350   47027    NA
3 36005 Bronx County, New York       211879   5751 1419250    NA
4 36007 Broome County, New York       19066   1290  197738    NA
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York   6786    535   76479    NA
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York        5499    528   75464    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence          8       1465609.
2 Low confidence          35         66228.
3 Moderate                19        306814.


In order to compare the average population of counties in each reliability category, I have to group each observation by their reliability category and then take the average of each grouping’s population estimate.
Using the same thresholds as before, the average population of high-confidence counties is 1,465,609, while the average population of low-confidence counties is 66,228. This suggests that larger counties are counted more accurately than smaller counties.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
The top 5 counties with the largest margins of error were Hamilton County, Wyoming County, Yates County, Washington County, and Greene County. Of these 5 counties, Washington had the largest population, totaling to almost 61,000 residents, while Hamilton County had the smallest population, totaling to about 5100. All 5 counties had margins of error above 16%, with Hamilton County having the largest margin of error at 34%. This suggests there is more accurate data collected about low-income women in larger counties (like those comprising New York City) than the smaller counties upstate. However, this is not surprising from a statistical standpoint. Unlike the Decennial Census, which aims to count everyone, the ACS makes estimates for a given geography based on sample data. Therefore, when the samples are smaller, each unit increase in the margin of error accounts for a much larger percentage than for a larger sample.
If a state agency were to allocate funding for economic development opportunities for women based on the percentage of low-income women as compiled by the ACS without accounting for margins of error, the agency might misjudge the extent of poverty as an issue for female residents in smaller counties versus larger counties. The 2023 ACS estimates that about 5% of Hamilton’s population were women whose income was below the poverty level in the past 12 months. However, the margin of error suggests that as much as 6.5% of Hamilton’s population may have been low-income women. Without taking into account the margin of error, however, the state agency might decide that Hamilton County doesn’t meet the minimum threshold required to be eligible for the funding.

title: Week 3: GGPLOT & Addressing Margins of Error
text: Went over the basic elements and syntax of using ggplot for data visualization. Discussed how to properly address margins of error in ACS data.

title: Week 3: GGPLOT & Addressing Margins of Error
text:
Key Concepts
Visualizing data is important because different datasets can have similar (or even identical) summary statistics but look very different (i.e. Ansombe’s Quartet).

A plot is a mapping from columns in a dataset to visual properties on a page. Known as “Grammer of Graphics” (“GG”).
Ex: estimate column -> position on y-axis, population column -> postition on x-axis

GGPLOT Basics plot1 <- ggplot(data) + this creates a blank canvas with your data as reference aes() + despite the name, “aesthetics” refers to column assignment geom_something() shape/type of chart
“Decorations” (i.e. colors, etc.) go in geom_*() portion of code, not aes()
Options for geom:

histogram
point (for scatterplot)
boxplot
col (for barchart)
line
errorbar

Combining 2 geom:

Each type has its own aes specfications
Ex: geom_col() has aes( x = somevalue, y = somevalue), while geom_errorbar() has aes(ymin = somevalue, ymax = somevalue)

Extra:

facet_wrap() for creating multiple charts side-by-side for comparison
coord_flip() to flip x and y axis orientation
mutate(str_remove(column, “__“)) to remove some text/edit a column
Can use theme_minimal() for graphs as a shortcut for nice aesthetics
labs() for the labels of a graph

Census Bureau uses coefficient of variation (“CV”).

CV is a relative measure of sampling error, tied to the 90% confidence interval.
Census assumes a low CV of 15% (high reliability), medium of 15-30%, and high > 30% (low reliability, high sampling error)

Derived uncertainty

Cannot simply add up or multiply margins of error when comparing different estimates
In tidycensus: moe_sum() will properly add moe’s for different estimates

Also: moe_prop() for one estimate as a share of another, and moe_ratio() for ratio of 2 variables


Change over time with ACS data

5-year ACS estimates have overlapping time periods when comparing years that are close together (ex: 2023 and 2022)
Instead, use ACS years that do not have overlapping periods (ex: 2018 and 2023)
Standard error of difference and confidence interval of change to determine if the difference in estimates between years is real (i.e. does not include zero)

title: Week 4: Working with Spatial Data in R
text:
Key Concepts
Overview of Geography & Coordinate Reference Systems

Geographic: latitude and longitude, measured in degrees

Geographers draw different ellipsoids to fit different areas of the Earth better
Ex: North American Datum 1927 (NAD27) based on Clarke’s ellipsoid from 1866
NAD83 based on satellite imagery; more accurate than NAD27 and most commonly used in U.S. today
WGS84 is the standard for GPS because it’s global

Projected: flattens 3D to 2D, measured in ft and meters

Projections distort shape, area, distance, and/or direction
Every projection has a “line of tangency” where there is no distortion
Cylindrical: northern and southern extremities of Earth most distorted - ex: Mercator
Conic: best for northern hemisphere (ex: Canada, U.S., Russia, China)
Planar: best for singular landmass (ex: Australia)

Projection for Philadelphia: PA southern state plane (2272)

Spatial features (Sf) and relevant commands in R:

st_crs(your data) to view crs of your data
st_set_crs() to add correct label (if missing)

if missing, may need to guess and check to find right crs

st_transform() to change the projection of your data
st_buffer() to create buffer around object

units will match that of the object/layer

st_intersects() is /not/ the same as st_touches()
st_filter() to select geographies that are completely within set buffer distance
st_union() to unify everything selected
st_intersection() to get common area
st_join() behaves like a left join for spatial datasets
st_distance() to returns a matrix of distances between all objects within 2 datasets
st_disjoint if geometries have no point in common (i.e. are completely separate)

section: Part 1: The same pull as Week 3, plus one argument

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
text:
Part 1b: Join by what
How much has income changed since 2015? Pull the older estimates. No geometry is needed, because this is just a table.

income_15 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  variables = c(med_inc_15 = "B19013_001"),
  year = 2015,
  output = "wide",
  geometry = FALSE
) %>%
  select(GEOID, med_inc_15E, med_inc_15M)

nrow(income_15)

[1] 384

nrow(philly_tracts)

[1] 391


Stop and look: The row counts are different. Before you join, predict why.
Row counts are different because the number of census tracts have changed in the past ~10 years.
Now join the 2015 table onto your tracts. The key is the column both tables share.

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(income_15, by = "GEOID")

nrow(philly_tracts)   # did the row count change?

[1] 391


The row count for philly_tracts did not change.
The rule: after every join, count rows and count NAs.

philly_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarize(
    n_tracts = n(),
    no_2015_match = sum(is.na(med_inc_15E))
  )

  n_tracts no_2015_match
1      391            35


Now look at which tracts failed to match:

# 2023 tracts with no 2015 partner
philly_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(is.na(med_inc_15E)) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME) %>%
  head(10)

         GEOID                                                   NAME
1  42101020702 Census Tract 207.02; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
2  42101012502 Census Tract 125.02; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
3  42101013701 Census Tract 137.01; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
4  42101016002 Census Tract 160.02; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
5  42101036901 Census Tract 369.01; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
6  42101013702 Census Tract 137.02; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
7  42101000101   Census Tract 1.01; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
8  42101000404   Census Tract 4.04; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
9  42101000805   Census Tract 8.05; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
10 42101000102   Census Tract 1.02; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania

# 2015 tracts with no 2023 partner: anti_join keeps rows with NO match
income_15 %>%
  anti_join(st_drop_geometry(philly_tracts), by = "GEOID") %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 3
   GEOID       med_inc_15E med_inc_15M
   <chr>             <dbl>       <dbl>
 1 42101018800       21949        5375
 2 42101020700       51268        8987
 3 42101013700       35033        4377
 4 42101000100       92207       16328
 5 42101001300       81250       18169
 6 42101016000       45030        8727
 7 42101036900       47083       16973
 8 42101038300       21500        8025
 9 42101014200       83924        4648
10 42101004102       34102        4092


Discuss as a team: Did these places move? What changed between 2015 and 2023? Why can’t left_join() fix this? Keep your answer in mind; Part 3 comes back to it.
Difference in tracts between 2023 and 2015; left_join() can’t fix missing/misaligned data.






Note



Some NAs aren’t boundary changes. A tract can match but have NA income because the Census suppressed the estimate. How would you tell the two kinds of NA apart?

In Part 1b, the join failed because it matched on a label (GEOID), and the label changed. st_join() matches on location instead: a row is matched to whatever it sits on top of. Stations don’t have a GEOID column, and they don’t need one.
Every station gets its tract’s attributes:

stations_with_tract <- st_join(stations, philly_tracts)

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
section: Part 4: How far is the nearest station?
text:
Part 4: How far is the nearest station?
st_distance() returns a matrix, not a column. Look at its shape first:

centroids <- st_centroid(st_geometry(philly_tracts))

dim(st_distance(centroids, stations))

[1] 391 319


Instead, find the nearest station for each tract, then measure only that one distance:

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(centroids, philly_tracts)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    dist_ft = as.numeric(
      st_distance(centroids, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)
    ),
    dist_mi = dist_ft / 5280
  )

summary(philly_tracts$dist_mi)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
 0.2161  2.6424  4.5875  5.1882  7.5316 15.2165      72

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
section: Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
text:
Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 2640) %>%
  st_union()

Pick whole cookies: which tracts don’t touch the zone at all?

outside_zone <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_filter(station_zone, .predicate = st_disjoint)

nrow(outside_zone)

[1] 162


Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

Notice: that last step is the left_join() from Part 1b. It’s a join by what (GEOID), used to bring a join-by-where result back into the table. The two kinds of join work together.

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
text:
Part 6: The Challenge
You now have three different definitions of “has access”:

Distance: the tract centroid is within X miles of a station (dist_mi)
Touch: the tract touches the half-mile zone at all (st_filter)
Coverage: at least Y% of the tract’s area is inside the zone (pct_covered)

Define “low-income.” For example, you could use the bottom quartile of tract median income, or a dollar threshold. Pick one and write it down.

Part 1 — Reconstructing the Data
In order to examine the article’s claims, I will look at tract-level data for the neighborhood of Mayfair, using the 5-year 2017 and 2022 ACS estimates for total population and foreign-born residents (variables B05002_001 and B05002_013, respectively). I will use tracts 332, 315.02, 315.01, 316, and 317 to estimate the neighborhood boundaries of Mayfair, as these census tract boundaries align with the neighborhood boundaries as depicted on Google Maps. Fortunately, these time periods (2013-2017 and 2018-2022) do not overlap, which will make the comparison more valid.
I will not look at the population change in Philadelphia between 2023 and 2024, as the Census Bureau does not list margins of error for those estimates and the time periods for these ACS estimates overlap, making any comparison more difficult to validate.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Part 3 — Adjudicating
Sorting the article’s claims into three buckets produces the following results:
Supported: There was a significant increase in the immigrant population in the neighborhood of Mayfair between 2017 and 2022. Taking into account the margins of error for each estimate in this analysis reveals that the difference between the two years is unlikely to be zero, given the z-score and the range of the confidence interval of the difference.
Not supported: Mayfair’s population did not significantly increase between 2017 and 2022. Analyzing the difference in the population estimates between the two years did not produce significant z-scores for any of the tracts, signaling that the changes in population estimates are unlikely to be non-zero.
Cannot be determined: It is unclear whether Philadelphia’s population significantly increased between 2023 and 2024. The Census Bureau does not list margins of error for those county-wide population estimates in the 5-year ACS data, therefore I cannot conduct the same analysis for this claim as I did for Mayfair. This also means that I can’t verify how Mayfair’s demographic changes compare to Philadelphia’s.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Part 4 — Rewriting the Claim
The neighborhood of Mayfair, in the 19149 ZIP code of Northeast Philadelphia, had about 26,601 residents in 2022. We can be moderately confident that about 34% of those residents were foreign-born. The immigrant population there grew by at least 1,431 people (about 28%) from 2013–2017 to 2018–2022, even though the neighborhood’s population on the whole did not significantly increase.
